author: Forbes
description:
When replacing just two tires on a vehicle, common consumer logic dictates placing the fresh rubber on the front axle—the end responsible for steering, heavy braking, and pulling the vehicle forward. To put this widespread assumption to the test, host Scotty Reiss joined Derek Secord, Senior Subjective Test Driver at Michelin, on a polished concrete wet skid pad engineered to induce hydroplaning.

Using two identical Toyota Camrys fitted with Michelin Defender 2 tires, the experiment compared a vehicle with new tires on the rear and 50% worn tires on the front against a vehicle with new tires on the front and worn tires on the rear. The results were both counter-intuitive and dramatic. When worn tires were placed on the front axle, hydroplaning caused predictable understeer. This provided immediate haptic feedback through the steering wheel, allowing the driver to simply lift off the throttle and regain control safely.
